Written Exam

Exam consisting of 8 learning test sections assessing knowledge and understanding of the
Organization Theory and Design topics.
Each section, not more than 25 minutes, will be independently graded
Threshold to pass is 18/30 an maximum Mark is 30/30.
The final mark is obtained as the average of marks given to each section of the written
exam: 0,25 rounded to the superior number
Each Test consists of 30 multiple choice questions with 4 possible alternatives.
Each correct answer adds 1 point, for each wrong answer you take off a point, if you do
not answer the score remains unchanged.
In some Tests some questions are replaced by twice as many statements that require you
to indicate as a true/false answer. For true/false answers you add or subtract 0.5.
Example of questions will be available for each Learning Test.

Sections of Learning Test are:
LEARNING TEST 1: Chapter 1 and 2
LEARNING TEST 2: Chapter 3
LEARNING TEST 3: Chapter 4, 5 and 6
LEARNING TEST 4: Chapter 7
LEARNING TEST 5: Chapter 8
LEARNING TEST 6: Chapter 9 and 10
LEARNING TEST 7: Chapter 11
LEARNING TEST 8: Chapter 12 and 13
There is the possibility to take the learning tests, 2 at a time, after the related topics have
been completed, during the course of Organization Theory and Design during the lessons.

The Basics

The “party” problem belongs to a class of
      resource allocation or constraint satisfaction problems

Can be modelled (and solved) in the abstract
                 through the very simple propositional logic

Although the constraints can get very complicated

When we reason, we do symbolic manipulation
                  the meaning of the symbols is irrelevant

KRR 2023-2024                                              26

Expressivity

While useful, propositional logic cannot represent
                                       all kinds of knowledge

Gives rise to many different representation languages
               different properties require different treatment

We cannot just make one big “unified” language
                                       for practical reasons

Impossible to study them all
               consider prototypical examples and extensions
KRR 2023-2024                                                27

Goal

Give you the tools to

   • understand when to use KR,
   • use it effectively, and
   • avoid unnecessary overhead

Question 1. Boolean Functions 5 P.
 1. How many ternary Boolean functions exist?

 2. Give an example of a propositional formula over the variables x, y, z which cannot
 be expressed as a propositional knowledge base. Justify your answer.

Solution 1.
 1. there are 28 = 256 different ternary Boolean functions: for each of the 8 different
 inputs we can choose to assign the value true or false

 2. x ∧ (y ∨ z) cannot be expressed as a conjunction of Horn clauses. The second clause
 is not Horn, and cannot be transformed to one.

Question 2. EL I 5 P.
Determine whether the following statements are true or false. Justify your answer or
provide a counter-example.

 1. For every EL concept C, there exists an interpretation that satisfies C

 2. For every EL concept C and every EL⊥ TBox T , there is a model of T with at
 least two elements that satisfies C

Solution 2.
 1. true: the trivial interpretation I = ({δ}, ·I ) where AI = {δ}, rI = {(δ, δ)} satisfies
 all EL concepts

 2. false: if the TBox is inconsistent, then there is no model of T

Question 3. EL II 5 P.
Consider the EL⊥ concepts

 C := A u ∃r.A u ∃s.B
 D := A u ∃r.(A u ∃s.>)
 E := ∃r.(A u ∃s.⊥)

 1. Determine whether the following subsumption relations hold without a TBox.
 Justify your answers.
 a) C v D
 b) D v E
 c) C u E v D

 2. Construct an EL⊥ TBox with only one GCI such that the three subsumption
 relations a), b) and c) hold.

Solution 3.
 1. a) false: can be seen that there is no homomorphism from the concept graph of
 D (depth

1)
 b) false: E ≡ ⊥ and D is satisfiable
 c) true: since E ≡ ⊥ the subsumption must always hold

 2. {> v ⊥}

Question 4. ALC 5 P.
 1. Using the tableau algorithm, show that the TBox

 T := {B v ¬(A u ∃r.¬B), A v ∃r.(A t ¬B)}

 is consistent.

 2. Build a satisfying model

 3. Rewrite T into a TBox containing only one GCI

Solution 4.
 1. It suffices to build one branch of the tableau, which remains open

 2. A simple model: one element, which belongs to neither A nor B

 3. > v (¬B t ¬(A u ∃r.¬B)) u (¬A t ∃r.(A t ¬B))

Question 5. Probabilistic Reasoning 5 P.
Consider the following probabilistic knowledge base:

 0.5 :: W oman ←
 0.5 :: F emale ←
 F emale ← W oman

 1. Under the independence assumption compute the probability of W oman and
 the probability of F emale

 2. In what kind of situations are these results reasonable?

 3. What would happen if we added 0.5 :: M ale ← ?

Solution 5.
 1. P (W oman) = 0.5; P (F emale) = 0.75

 2. there are females that are not women (e.g., if we are encoding a class of species,
 or dividing by age)

 3. the probability of being Male and Female is positive (in fact 3/8). Other solutions
 were also accepted, as long as they were justified

Question 6. Temporal Logic 5 P.
Consider the LTLf formula
 ϕ := ¬a U (¬ > ∨ a)

 1. Build a temporal model M of ϕ such that M, 0 |= ¬a or explain why it is not
 possible.

 2. Build a temporal model M of ϕ such that M, 1 |= a and M, 2 |= ¬a or explain why
 it is not possible.

Solution 6.
For both questions, the model ¬a, a, ¬a satisfies the condition.

 In fact, the formula ϕ is a tautology. Any temporal interpretation satisfies it. The
main point was to build the interpretations.

Question 7. Extra (+3 P.)
Joe Montana once said

 If you ain’t cheating, you ain’t trying. And they are trying hard.

 1. Encode this knowledge using any KR language of your choice, and decide whether
 “they” are cheating or not.

 2. Can you say whether they are cheating hard ?

Solution 7.
 1. By counterpositive, we can express

 cheating ← trying trying ←

 and from this we can deduce cheating as a consequence

 2. we have not seen any knowledge constructor for handling modifiers. As it is stated,
 the knowledge does not express whether trying hard implies cheating hard.

Question 5. DLs 4 P.
 1. Explain the notion of a nominal.

 2. Argue why it is impossible to express nominals in EL⊥

Solution 5.
A nominal is a concept that contains only one object. It cannot be expressed in EL⊥
because the disjoint union of models is a model (violating the condition for nominals).

## Modeling reflexivity

Modeling reflexivity for `loves`. Intuitively this should work:
```
loves(X, X).
```
This fact (i.e., rule without a body) is however *usafe*.
DLV requires that variables that appear in the head of a rule (like `X` in
`loves(X, X)`) also appear in a positive predicate in the body of the rule
(i.e., a predicate not under the scope of negation as failure).

We can fix the rule as follows:
`loves(X, X) :- person(X). % SAFE`

## Modeling asymmetry and irreflexivity

Add a constraint that enforces that `parent_of` is asymmetric.
Meaning: whenever `parent_of(X, Y)`, then it is impossible that `parent_of(Y, X)`.
Or: `parent_of(X, Y)` and `parent_of(Y, X)` cannot be true at the same time:
```
:- parent_of(X, Y), parent_of(Y, X).
```

`parent_of` is irreflexive:
```
:- parent_of(X, X).
```

## Modeling functionality

The predicate `spouse` is functional if every `X` has at most one spouse, i.e.,
whenever `spouse(X, Y)` and `spouse(X, Z)` are true, then `Y` and `Z` must be
equal: `Y = Z`.

This would suggest the following solution:
`Y = Z :- spouse(X, Y), spouse(X, Z).`
This is however incorrect, since Datalog/DLV does not support equality in the
head of a rule.

Equivalently, we can express that it is impossible for an `X` to have spouses
`Y` and `Z` different from each other at the same time, with a constraint:
```
:- spouse(X, Y), spouse(X, Z), Y != Z.
```

This means that if in our KB we have:
```
spouse(alice, bob).
spouse(alice, david).
```
Then DLV is going to give an empty output: the KB is inconsistent.

However, what if we have `spouse(alice, bob).` and `spouse(alice, robert).`?
We could imagine that `bob` and `robert` are different *names* for the same
person, and so our KB should not be inconsistent.

Datalog however assumes the *unique name assumption*: constants with a different
name refer to different things/entities. So, according to Datalog, `bob` and
`robert` must be different people.

We can try to circumvent this assumption by removing the constraint above
(i.e., `:- spouse(X, Y), spouse(X, Z), Y != Z.`), and instead modeling our own
equality relation, defining the predicate `same_as` as an equivalence relation
(reflexive, symmetric, and transitive):
```
same_as(X, X) :- person(X). % Reflexivity
same_as(X, Y) :- same_as(Y, X). % Symmetry
same_as(X, Y) :- same_as(X, Z), same_as(Z, Y). % Transitivity
```

Now we can model functionality as follows:
`same_as(Y, Z) :- spouse(X, Y), spouse(X, Z).`

So, if we have
```
spouse(alice, bob).
spouse(alice, robert).
```
then DLV will infer `same_as(bob, robert)`.

Exercise 1.2

Program P: `p :- not p.`

Candidates:

- `S1 = {}`: NOT an AS.
 Taking the GL(P, S1), we delete `not p` from the body, and all that is left is `p.`
 S1 is not a model of GL(P, S1), because it does not satisfy the fact `p` => not an answer set.

- `S2 = {p}`: NOT an AS
 Taking the GL of P = `p :- not p.`,
 because the body of the only rule contains `not p`,
 and `p` is in our candidate solution S2,
 then we must remove the whole rule `p :- not p.`, so that
 `GL(P, S2)` is an empty program: a program with no facts and rules.

 Is S2 an answer set of `GL(P, S2)`?
 1. Is S2 a model of the GL(P, S2)? True, because there is nothing to
 satisfy, so all the rules of GL(P, S2) are trivially/vacuously satisfied.
 2. Consistency: S2 is consistent.
 3. S2 is not however NOT an AS because of minimality: a proper subset of S2,
 namely the empty set {}, is alrready an answer set of GL(P, S2).

 VERY IMPORTANT NOTE:
 The fact that the empty set {} is an answer set of GL(P, S2)
 does NOT mean that {} is an answer set of the whole initial program P.

 REMEMBER THE GENERAL RULE:
 If X is an answer set of GL(P, X), then it is an answer set of the whole program P.
 <-- Note that the candidate answer set and the set used to compute the GL
 of P MUST BE THE SAME in order for this rule to work (X in this case).

 So, in order for {} to be an answer set of the program p, it should be an answer set of GL(P, {})!
 But we have already seen that S1={} is not an answer set of GL(P, S1) =
 GL(P, {}). So {} cannot be an answer set!

 ---> The fact that {} is an answer set of GL(P, S2), i.e. of the program <---
 ---> obtained by taking the GL of P with respect to a *different* candidate S2, <---
 ---> does not tell us anything. <---

Another candidate:
- `S3 = {-p}`: Not an answer set.
 GL(P, S3): Delete `not p` (because `p` is not in S3), and so we are left
 with simply `p`. S3 is not a model of the GL(P, S3).

Note: Sometimes there are no answer sets for a program!

Exercise 3

Program P:
`a :- not b.`

Candidates (going brute-force again):

- S1 = {}: NOT an answer set.
 GL(P, S1): Considering the only rule `a :- not b`,
 because `b` is not in S1,
 then `b` "fails" to be true,
 so `not b` is true, meaning that we can remove it from the rule.
 All we are left with is the program `GL(P, S1)` = {`a.`}
 S1 is not a model of the resulting program.

- S2 = {a}: YES, an answer set.
 GL(P, S2): {a}
 S2 is a model, it is consistent, and it is minimal.

- S3 = {b}
 GL(P, S3).
 Considering the only rule `a :- not b`,
 Since `b` is inside S3,
 then `not b` is false.
 The whole rule `a :- not b` is true/satisfied, since its body is
 satisfied. So we can forget about it, and delete it.
 The resulting program GL(P, S3) is the empty program, and
 S3 = {b} is not a *minimal* model, since the empty set is a model of
 the empty program.

- S4 = {a, b}
 GL(P, S4) = {}
 S4 = {a, b} is not a *minimal* model, again.

To sum up: the only answer set is S2 = {a}.

Exercise 9

```
p :- not p, d .
q v r :- not d.
d :- not r.
-q.
```

Let's build our candidate answer set step by step.
For sure, we start by adding the fact: `S = {-q}`. We can now try reasoning
rule-by-rule, since going brute-force would take too long.

- Consider `p :- not p, d .`
 - What if we add `p` to our candidate `S`? Then this rule will be deleted during the GL.
 We will thus have `p` inside our solution `S`, but p will be nowhere else in the resulting program.
 If the candidate S will be a model of GL(P, S), it won't then be
 minimal, as it will contain {p}, but its presence will not be needed to
 satisfy any rule. So:
 ===> our candidate S should NOT include p.
 - If p is not in S then, during the GL of our program, we are going to
 delete `not p` from the first rule, which becomes `p :- d.`
 Should we include `d` or not? If we do, then we must also satisfy the
 head `p` -> contradiction/circularity, since we started by assuming that
 `p` should not be in `S`. So:
 =====> we should NOT include `d` in our candidate
 - So, for the next rule
 `q v r :- not d.`
 Since we must not have `d` in our solution, when we apply the GL we would be
 left with just `q v r `.
 We cannot chose `q`, since our set S contain the fact `-q`. SO
 ===> we need to satisfy `r`
 Updating our candidate -> `S = {-q, r}`
- Consider the final rule: `d :- not r.`.
 This rule will be eliminated during the GL, since `r` is in our candidate
 solution. There is nothing else to do.

Final candidate: `S = {-q, r}`

You can check that this is indeed an answer set by computing `GL(P, {-q, r})`.

Are there any other answer sets? No. It's the only answer set, because there
were not other choices that we could have made during the construction of the
candidate S.

## QUERY 9

Retrieve all ancestors (i.e., parents of parents of parents of parents...) of
:david (hint: use property paths).

```sparql
SELECT ?ancestor WHERE { ?ancestor :parentOf+ :david . }
```
intuitively this says
```sparql
SELECT ?ancestor WHERE {
 { ?ancestor :parentOf :david . }
 UNION
 { ?ancestor :parentOf/:parentOf :david . }
 UNION
 { ?ancestor :parentOf/:parentOf/:parentOf :david . }
 UNION
 { ?ancestor :parentOf/:parentOf/:parentOf/:parentOf :david . }
 ...
 # To the infinity
 }
```
Of course we cannot write an infinite UNION query to cover all sequences of
`:parentOf` predicates of arbitrary length, so `+` is not just an abbreviation.

Besides *SELECT* queries, there are other query types. E.g.,
*CONSTRUCT*

To build/construct a graph containing all the ancestors of `:david`
```
CONSTRUCT {?x :ancestorOf :david } WHERE {?x :parentOf+ :david }
```
The result of a CONSTRUCT query is not a table, but an RDF graph (in Turtle or
other formats).

Reminder. Intuitively:
- `:parentOf+` is the transitive closure of `:parentOf`
- `:parentOf*` is the reflexive-transitive closure of `:parentOf`

# rdf:type vs rdfs:subClassOf

Let's say that
 :Student represents the set Student = {carol, alice}
 :Person represents the set Person = {carol, alice, bob}

:Student rdfs:subClassOf :Person
means that
 Student ⊆ Person
I.e., Student is a subset of Person,
i.e., every element of Student is also an element of Person

:carol rdf:type :Student
means that
 carol ∈ Student
i.e., carol is an element of Student

:Student rdf:type :Person
would mean that
 Student ∈ Person
i.e., the set Student is an element of the set Person
Which is incorrect

# Domain and range

Let's say :purchase represents the binary relation
purchase = { (alice, animals),
 (bob, meddle) }

(which can be represented as
 :alice :purchase :animals .
 :bob :purchase :meddle . )

Then:
domain(purchase) = {alice, bob}
range(purchase) = {animals, meddle}

:purchase rdfs:domain :Person
means that the domain of purchase is Person,
which means that
 domain(purchase) = {alice, bob} ⊆ Person
and so
-> alice ∈ Person (:alice rdf:type :Person)
-> bob ∈ Person (:bob rdf:type :Person)

:purchase rdfs:range :MusicAlbum
means that the range of purchase is the set MusicAlbum
which means that
 range(purchase) = {animals, meddle} ⊆ MusicAlbum
and so
-> animals ∈ MusicAlbum (:animals rdf:type :MusicAlbum)
-> meddle ∈ MusicAlbum (:meddle rdf:type :MusicAlbum)

 How to express in DL that Alice and Bob are the only children of Carol?
 We already know hasChild(carol, alice) and hasChild(carol, bob).

 The expression
 ∀hasChild.{alice, bob}
 denotes the class of entities all of whose children are inside the set {alice, bob}
 In other words, if x belongs to ∀hasChild.{alice, bob} and y is a child of
 x, then y must belong to the set {alice, bob}, which means that y=alice or y=bob.

 To state that carol belongs to this class we can use a DL concept assertion:
 ∀hasChild.{alice, bob}(carol)
 Or we define some class C = ∀hasChild.{alice, bob}
 and then say C(carol).

 So, together with the facts above (hasChild(carol, alice) and
 hasChild(carol, bob)), the assertion C(carol) lets us express that alice and
 bob are children of carol, and her *only* children.

## OWL/DL Geo Ontology Modeling

### Expressing functionality and inverse functionality in DL

Express that `partOf` is functional using DL syntax.
"`partOf` is functional" means:
- Every entity is linked to at most one thing through `partOf`
- I.e., every entity is `partOf` at most one thing
- I.e., if something is an entity, then it is `partOf` at most one thing
In DL:
```
⊤ ⊑ ≤1 partOf.⊤
```

Express that `capitalOf` is inverse functional using DL syntax:
`⊤ ⊑ ≤1 capitalOf-.⊤`
In this case we use `-` to take the inverse of the `capitalOf` relation, and
then the axiom is the same as functionality.

Another way to see it: `capitalOf` being inverse functional means that any
entity has at most one capital. So we could define `hasCapital` as the inverse
of `capitalOf`:
 `hasCapital = capitalOf-`
And then say that `hasCapital` is functional:
 `⊤ ⊑ ≤1 hasCapital.⊤`
If we substitute `hasCapital` with its definition (`capitalOf-`), we get again
the inverse functionality axiom for `capitalOf`.
 `⊤ ⊑ ≤1 capitalOf-.⊤`

### DL: ranges and local ranges

Express ranges in DL: the range of `genericPartOf` is `GeoEntity`
```
⊤ ⊑ ∀ genericPartOf.GeoEntity
```

Local ranges:
The range of `genericPartOf` is `Region` for `City`. I.e.:
If something is a `City`, then it can only be a `genericPartOf` a `Region`
```
City ⊑ ∀ genericPartOf.Region
```

Similarly:
The range of `genericPartOf` is `Country` for `Region`. I.e.:
If something is a `Region`, then it can only be a `genericPartOf` a `Country`
```
Region ⊑ ∀ genericPartOf.Country
```

Similarly:
The range of `genericPartOf` is `Continent` for `Country`. I.e.:
If something is a `Country`, then it can only be a `genericPartOf` a `Continent`
```
Country ⊑ ∀ genericPartOf.Continent
```

Exercise 3 fixing the inconsistent ontology

Why is the ontology inconsistent? Because of this axiom:
```
HappyParent = ∀ hasChild.HappyPerson
```

```
∀ hasChild.HappyPerson
```
is the set of entities such that all of their children are happy people.

But what if an entity does not have any children? Then trivially all of their
children are happy people, and by the axiom above they must be an `HappyParent`.
Which of course does not make sense.

Different ways to fix the ontology:
```
HappyParent = Parent ⊓ ∀ hasChild.HappyPerson (where Parent = ∃ hasChild.⊤)
HappyParent = ∃ hasChild.⊤ ⊓ ∀ hasChild.HappyPerson
HappyParent = ∃ hasChild.Person ⊓ ∀ hasChild.HappyPerson
```

In general, avoid this kind of axiom:
```
C = ∀ R.D
```

Note:
```
HappyParent = ∀ hasChild.HappyPerson
```
is an abbreviation for
```
HappyParent ⊑ ∀ hasChild.HappyPerson
HappyParent ⊒ ∀ hasChild.HappyPerson
```

The first of these inclusions is OK:
```
HappyParent ⊑ ∀ hasChild.HappyPerson
```
means that if something is an `HappyParent`, then all of their children are
`HappyPerson`s

The second inclusion is the problem:
```
HappyParent ⊒ ∀ hasChild.HappyPerson
```
Means that if all of the children of an entity are `HappyPerson`s, then this
entity is an `HappyParent`. This is the source of the issues above.

So again, the way to fix the axiom is:
```
HappyParent ⊒ Parent ⊓ ∀ hasChild.HappyPerson
```
Where `Parent = ∃ hasChild.⊤`.

A Sudoku puzzle consists of a 9x9 grid, in which each cell must contain a number between 1 and 9,
according to the following rules:
 • Each row must contain exactly one instance of each number (no repetitions on rows)
 • Each column must contain exactly one instance of each number (no repetitions on columns)
 • The grid is divided in 9 3x3 sub-grids: each sub-grid must contain exactly one instance of
 each number (no repetitions on sub-grids)
You can assume that the input to the function is given in the form of a matrix indexed as:
 individual[row][column]

maximum capacity) with items from a list, maximizing the total value of the knapsack but without
exceeding the capacity. There is a single copy of each item and each item has a weight and value.
You can assume that the input to the function is given in the form of:
 • A maximum weight (integer) capacity

 • An array of values, indexed as values[i]

1. A Document Collection: A static set of documents (the corpus) to be searched.

2. A Set of Topics (Queries): A set of formal descriptions of information needs (often including a title,
               description, and narrative) that represent what a user might search for.

3. Relevance Judgments (Ground Truth): A binary or graded list indicating which documents are
               relevant to which topics.
           These components are typically created through a rigorous process, such as those used by TREC (Text
           REtrieval Conference). First, documents are crawled or gathered to form the corpus. Then, domain
           experts or organizers formulate the queries. Crucially, the relevance judgments are created by human
           assessors. Since it is impossible to judge millions of documents for every query, a technique called
           Pooling is often used: the top k results from various different search systems are merged into a "pool,"
           and only these documents are judged by humans. Any document not in the pool is assumed to be
           irrelevant.
           Regarding the second part of the question, Precision@1 (P@1) is the preferred metric for Navigational
           Queries (or Known-Item Search). A classic example is a user searching for "Facebook login" or asking a
           digital assistant (like Siri) "What is the capital of Italy?". In these specific tasks, the user has a single,
           correct destination in mind or requires one specific fact. The user experience is binary: if the first result is
           correct, the system succeeds; if the user has to scroll to the second result, the system has failed to
           provide the instant access expected. Therefore, measuring how often the very first item is relevant is the
           only metric that truly reflects user satisfaction in this context.

1. Initialization: A random selection of observations from the dataset is made to serve as
   the initial centroids for the current iteration.

2. Assignment: Each observation is assigned to the cluster whose centroid is most similar
(closest in distance) to the observation itself.

3. Convergence Check: If no observations are reassigned to a different cluster compared to
the previous step, the algorithm terminates, having reached convergence.

4. Update and Iteration: Otherwise, a new centroid is calculated for each cluster as the
mathematical average of all observations currently belonging to it. The process then
returns to Step 2.

This algorithm is highly sensitive to outliers, which can significantly skew the average
values and displace centroids from their optimal positions. Conducting a thorough data
cleaning process beforehand is strongly recommended.

 Traditional methodological approach 1

Assuming a common time unit (e.g., daily, weekly, monthly), let m represent average
spending, f average purchase frequency, and t the average customer lifetime. Customer
revenue (r) is then obtained as r = m × f.

 CLTV = r*t = (mf)*t

In order to distinguish revenues from profits, we define p as the company’s profit margin and
explicitly include it in the Customer Lifetime Value (CLTV) formulation:

 CLTV = r*t*p = ((mf)*t*p)

Then we can introduce the discount rate i, an interest applied to reduce future cash flows
(e.g. usually around 10% per year) and a churn rate c, i.e. the percentage of customers who
leaving the company in the period:

an automatic (programmed) player.

(and hence conquer the castle).

                 • a tower, which can hit the attackers;

                 • a barracks, which can train units;

;Bart tells you that Rex and Dave are both knights or both knaves. 
;Dave tells you that Zoey is a knave. 
;Rex claims, “Bart is a knave.” 
;Zoey claims, “Rex is a knight and Dave is a knave.”

(declare-datatypes () ((I b d r z)))
(declare-fun Knight (I) Bool) ; to be a knight
(declare-fun Knave (I) Bool) ; to be a knave
(assert (forall ((x I)) (= (Knight x) (not (Knave x)))))

(assert (= (Knight b) (or (and (Knight r) (Knight d)) (and (Knave r) (Knave d)))))
(assert (= (Knight d) (Knave z)))
(assert (= (Knight r) (Knave b)))
(assert (= (Knight z) (and (Knight r) (Knave d))))

(check-sat)
(get-value ((Knight b) (Knight d) (Knight r) (Knight z)))

;uniqueness of solution
(assert (not (and (Knave b) (Knave d) (Knight r) (Knight z))))
(check-sat)
